title: Selberg Density Axiom Bug Discovery
content: Identifies a threshold bug in the parent file: the `selberg_density_axiom` claims every interval $(l!, (l+1)!]$ for $l \ge 3$ contains a prime $p$ where $p - k!$ is composite for all $k$ with $k! < p$. This is false for $l = 3$: exhaustive checking shows all 6 primes in $(6, 24]$ fail the condition. The correct threshold is $l \ge 4$, where $p = 101 \in (24, 120]$ is the first qualifying prime.
mathContext: The condition `AllFactorialSubtractionsComposite$(p)$: $\forall k: k! < p \Rightarrow (p - k!)$ is composite and $\ge 2$. For $p \in (6, 24]$: the primes $7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23$ all have $p - 2$ or $p - 6$ prime, violating the condition.

title: Exhaustive Counterexample for l = 3
content: Six theorems, one for each prime in $(6, 24]$, each proving failure by exhibiting a factorial index $k$ where $p - k!$ is prime. The pattern: $p = 7, 13, 19$ fail at $k = 2$ ($p - 2$ is prime), while $p = 11, 17, 23$ fail at $k = 3$ ($p - 6$ is prime). All proofs use `norm_num` to verify primality of the offending difference.
mathContext: Failure witnesses: $7 - 2! = 5$ (prime), $11 - 3! = 5$ (prime), $13 - 2! = 11$ (prime), $17 - 3! = 11$ (prime), $19 - 2! = 17$ (prime), $23 - 3! = 17$ (prime). The factorials $2! = 2$ and $3! = 6$ create differences that land on primes too frequently in this small interval.

title: p = 101 Qualifies in I(4)
content: Proves that 101 is the first qualifying prime: $101 \in (24, 120]$ and all factorial subtractions yield composites. The proof bounds $k \le 4$ (since $5! = 120 > 101$), then checks $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ with `interval_cases` and `norm_num`. Key factorizations: $101 - 1 = 100 = 4 \times 25$, $101 - 2 = 99 = 9 \times 11$, $101 - 6 = 95 = 5 \times 19$, $101 - 24 = 77 = 7 \times 11$.
mathContext: For $p = 101$: $p - 0! = p - 1! = 100 = 2^2 \cdot 5^2$, $p - 2! = 99 = 3^2 \cdot 11$, $p - 3! = 95 = 5 \cdot 19$, $p - 4! = 77 = 7 \cdot 11$. All composite and $\ge 2$. Since $5! = 120 > 101$, no further conditions apply.

title: Corrected Selberg Density Axiom (l ≥ 4)
content: States the corrected axiom: for $l \ge 4$, the interval $(l!, (l+1)!]$ contains at least one qualifying prime. Verified for $l = 4$ (with $p = 101$). The general case $l \ge 5$ requires the Brun-Titchmarsh inequality and Selberg sieve, both absent from Mathlib.
mathContext: The Brun-Titchmarsh inequality bounds $\pi(x; q, a) \le \frac{2x}{\phi(q)\log(x/q)}$ for primes in arithmetic progressions. For factorial intervals with $l \ge 4$, the density of primes is sufficient to guarantee at least one avoids all factorial residues.

title: Infinitely Many Qualifying Primes
content: Proves the main theorem: for any $n$, there exists $p > n$ that is prime and qualifying. Uses the corrected axiom with $l = n + 4 \ge 4$, giving $p \in ((n+4)!, (n+5)!]$. Since $(n+4)! \ge n + 4 > n$, we get $p > n$ via `Nat.self_le_factorial`. Includes summary of the bug fix and remaining infrastructure gaps (Brun-Titchmarsh, Selberg sieve).
mathContext: For any $n$: set $l = n + 4$. The corrected axiom gives $p > (n+4)! \ge n + 4 > n$. The qualifying primes grow at least as fast as $(n+4)!$, far exceeding polynomial growth.
